subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 28-year-old woman, 3 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, feels tearful and fatigued and has a depressed affect. She is otherwise able to care for herself and her newborn, and her symptoms began 2 days ago. She has no prior psychiatric history.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Postpartum blues affect 50-85% of women, beginning 2-3 days after delivery with depressed affect, tearfulness, and fatigue, and usually resolve within 2 weeks. Treatment is supportive, with follow-up to assess for possible MDD with peripartum onset. The absence of psychotic features and the brief, self-limited course distinguish this from more serious peripartum mood disorders.

explanation_incorrect.A: MDD with peripartum onset lasts 2 weeks or longer with more severe, persistent depressive symptoms and functional impairment, not the brief self-limited tearfulness here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Postpartum psychosis involves mood-congruent delusions, hallucinations, or thoughts of harming the baby or self, all of which are absent in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.D: GAD requires excessive worry most days for at least 6 months with CRIMES symptoms, not brief postpartum tearfulness starting 2 days ago.
explanation_incorrect.E: Adjustment disorder requires symptoms within 3 months of a stressor with marked distress; the classic brief 2-3 day course after delivery points to postpartum blues.

educationalObjective: Postpartum blues are common, begin 2-3 days after delivery, resolve within 2 weeks, and require supportive care with follow-up for MDD.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 32-year-old woman presents 3 weeks after delivery with persistent depressed mood, anhedonia, fatigue, and feelings of worthlessness for the past 3 weeks. She has difficulty caring for the infant and reports no delusions or hallucinations. She has a history of a major depressive episode before pregnancy.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Postpartum blues; supportive care and reassurance
MDD with peripartum onset; CBT and an SSRI
Postpartum psychosis; hospitalization and an atypical antipsychotic

explanation_correct: MDD with peripartum onset (formerly called postpartum depression) occurs in 10-15%, meets full MDD criteria with onset during pregnancy or within 4 weeks after delivery, and is treated first line with CBT and SSRIs. The 3-week duration, functional impairment, and prior mood disorder history distinguish it from self-limited blues. No psychotic features are present, so this is not postpartum psychosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Postpartum blues are brief (starting 2-3 days after delivery and resolving within 2 weeks) and lack marked functional impairment; this patient needs active treatment.
explanation_incorrect.B: Adjustment disorder with benzodiazepines is not indicated; benzodiazepines are not first-line for peripartum depression.
explanation_incorrect.D: Postpartum psychosis requires delusions, hallucinations, or thoughts of harming the baby or self; none are present, and it would require hospitalization.
explanation_incorrect.E: GAD is dominated by excessive worry with CRIMES symptoms, not a full depressive episode with anhedonia and worthlessness.

educationalObjective: MDD with peripartum onset meets full MDD criteria within 4 weeks of delivery and is treated first line with CBT and SSRIs.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 24-year-old primigravida, 10 days postpartum, believes the baby is possessed and hears voices telling her the infant would be better off dead. She has a family history of bipolar disorder and recently changed her medication. She is disorganized and intermittently tearful with mood-congruent beliefs.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this condition and its management?

options.text: Postpartum psychosis with mood-congruent features; hospitalization and an atypical antipsychotic
Postpartum blues; supportive care and outpatient follow-up
MDD with peripartum onset; start an SSRI as an outpatient
Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor; observation only
Obsessive-compulsive disorder; exposure and response prevention

explanation_correct: Postpartum psychosis occurs in 0.1-0.2% and features mood-congruent delusions, hallucinations, and thoughts of harming the baby or self. Risk factors include first pregnancy, family history, bipolar disorder, psychotic disorder, and recent medication change, all present here. Treatment is hospitalization with initiation of an atypical antipsychotic; ECT may be used if insufficient. This is a psychiatric emergency.

explanation_incorrect.B: Postpartum blues are brief, self-limited, and lack psychotic features; command hallucinations and delusions require emergency care.
explanation_incorrect.C: MDD with peripartum onset lacks psychotic features; delusions and command hallucinations make this psychosis, not unipolar depression.
explanation_incorrect.D: Brief psychotic disorder does not capture the mood-congruent postpartum picture, and observation alone is unsafe given infanticidal ideation.
explanation_incorrect.E: OCD can involve intrusive thoughts of harming the infant, but these are ego-dystonic without true delusions or hallucinations; here the beliefs are mood-congruent and psychotic.

educationalObjective: Postpartum psychosis involves mood-congruent delusions/hallucinations and thoughts of harming baby or self, requires hospitalization and an atypical antipsychotic, and is more likely with first pregnancy, bipolar or psychotic history, or recent medication change.
